step1_summary: Chief complaint: Progressive difficulty hearing in the LEFT ear for ~6 weeks.

Symptoms: • Onset 6 weeks ago, intermittent. • Unilateral (left) hearing loss. • Intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in the left ear—improves when TV/music is on (masking). • Occasional light-headedness/“off-balance” sensation, mild, not true vertigo, no associated chest pain, palpitations, or nausea. • No ear pain, no otorrhea, no pruritus, no fever.
Past medical history: Previously had a brief (2-day) episode of hearing difficulty about 1 year ago; otherwise none mentioned.
Family / Social history: Not discussed (no alcohol, smoking or occupational noise exposure mentioned).
Vital signs / Exam findings: None obtained during video visit.
Labs / Imaging: None to date; face-to-face otoscopic exam planned to rule out cerumen impaction or other external/middle-ear pathology.

V: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss secondary to labyrinthine artery ischemia: unilateral acute/subacute loss ± tinnitus/dizziness.
I: Viral labyrinthitis/neuritis: can cause unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, mild dizziness without fever.
Serous otitis media/Eustachian-tube dysfunction (post-URTI inflammation): conductive loss, aural fullness, tinnitus.
N: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma): slow, progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, disequilibrium.
Cholesteatoma: chronic unilateral conductive loss with tinnitus; possible dizziness.
D: Presbycusis/age-related degeneration: sensorineural loss and tinnitus, but patient only 32 y/o making this less likely.
I2: Ototoxic drug effect (e.g., aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, chemotherapy): no medication history given but always a consideration.
C: Congenital ossicular malformation or cochlear malformation—possible but would present much earlier.
A: Autoimmune inner-ear disease: fluctuating unilateral loss and tinnitus possible.
T: Barotrauma/physical trauma to ear: can produce unilateral loss and tinnitus; no history reported.
E: Menière’s disease (endolymphatic hydrops): episodic tinnitus, unilateral fluctuating hearing loss, and vertigo/disequilibrium.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Most common, easily reversible cause of unilateral hearing loss; clinician specifically planning otoscopy to rule it out first.
supporting_evidence: Gradual unilateral muffled hearing over weeks.
No pain, discharge, or infection signs.
Intermittent nature possible if wax shifts in canal.
opposing_evidence: Patient denies cotton-bud use (but wax can still occur).
Mild dizziness less typical though can occur via pressure effects.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic triad includes unilateral fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo; patient has two of three features (loss + tinnitus) with some disequilibrium.
supporting_evidence: Intermittent tinnitus relieved by background noise (common coping behaviour).
opposing_evidence: Vertigo described as mild light-headedness, not classic room-spinning severe episodes.
Symptoms continuous for 6 weeks rather than discrete attacks lasting minutes–hours.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Inflammatory middle-ear effusion can cause unilateral muffled hearing, tinnitus and mild imbalance.
supporting_evidence: Conductive nature fits muffled hearing description.
No pain or fever—consistent with non-infective effusion.
opposing_evidence: No recent URI or nasal symptoms reported.
Adult unilateral effusion less common without other triggers.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Slowly progressive unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus and imbalance; important not to miss even if rare.
opposing_evidence: Relatively short duration (6 weeks) — tumours usually progress over months/years.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can produce unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and dizziness, often post-viral.
supporting_evidence: Triad of auditory and vestibular symptoms.
opposing_evidence: Lack of antecedent URI or acute onset; symptoms more chronic than typical viral course.
